title: Trump Announces U.S. Control of Part of Venezuela’s Vast Oil Reserves
shortdescription: President Donald Trump says the United States has secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private companies, in a major effort to revive the country’s energy industry and increase U.S. oil supplies.

description.subtitle: U.S. Announces Major Venezuela Oil Agreement
description.text: President Donald Trump has announced an unprecedented agreement under which the United States will take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves, representing roughly one-fifth of the country’s vast petroleum resources. Trump said the arrangement was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in cooperation with Venezuela’s interim government and private-sector companies. The agreement is intended to revive Venezuela’s severely weakened oil industry while increasing supplies of crude available to U.S. refiners. Trump presented the initiative as a major energy and economic opportunity, saying it would not require American taxpayers to finance the investment. Under the proposed arrangement, private companies would provide capital and expertise to restore production from oil fields in regions including the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo. Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude reserves, but years of underinvestment, deteriorating infrastructure, sanctions and political instability have sharply reduced its ability to produce and export oil. The agreement therefore represents a significant shift in Washington’s approach to Venezuelan energy resources. Rather than simply restricting Venezuela’s oil industry through sanctions, the Trump administration is seeking to place American businesses at the center of efforts to rebuild production. Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez has backed the initiative, arguing that increased investment could help restore the country’s economy. The precise legal and ownership structure of the arrangement remains unclear, however, leaving important questions about how U.S. control would operate and how revenues would ultimately be distributed. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

description.subtitle: Private Investment Expected to Rebuild Oil Industry
description.text: The agreement is built around an enormous investment program intended to repair and modernize Venezuela’s damaged petroleum infrastructure. Venezuelan officials have projected that the initiative could attract approximately $100 billion in private investment and generate around $209 billion in tax revenue for the Venezuelan government. The proposed development would focus on 17 oil fields and is expected to involve American energy companies and other private-sector operators with the technology and capital needed to restore production. Venezuela’s oil industry has struggled for years with aging facilities, insufficient maintenance, declining investment and limited access to advanced equipment. Its heavy crude resources are particularly difficult to develop because they require specialized production and refining infrastructure. Bringing output back to previous levels could therefore require substantial capital and take several years. Trump has emphasized the potential benefits for U.S. consumers, arguing that increased Venezuelan production could help reduce gasoline prices and strengthen American energy supplies. The administration is also seeking to replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve after years of relatively low inventories. Greater access to Venezuelan crude could be strategically valuable because U.S. Gulf Coast refineries are equipped to process heavy crude grades similar to those produced in Venezuela. The deal could consequently create commercial opportunities for American refiners while providing Venezuela with much-needed investment. Nevertheless, energy analysts have warned that the projected benefits will not appear immediately. Venezuela’s production capacity cannot be restored simply through a change in ownership or policy. Major infrastructure repairs, new drilling, upgraded processing facilities and improvements to export terminals would all be required. The scale of the proposed investment demonstrates the administration’s long-term ambitions, but the eventual economic impact will depend on how quickly those projects can be implemented. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

description.subtitle: Oil Market Impact Could Take Years
description.text: Although the agreement involves an enormous volume of oil reserves, its immediate effect on global energy markets is expected to be limited because Venezuela cannot rapidly transform its reserves into additional production. The country has more than 300 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, but much of its petroleum infrastructure has deteriorated after years of economic crisis and underinvestment. Production facilities, pipelines, refineries and export terminals require extensive rehabilitation before Venezuela can significantly increase output. The country's heavy crude also requires specialized processing, further limiting the speed at which new production can reach international markets. Trump has linked the initiative to his efforts to lower U.S. gasoline prices and improve energy security, but analysts caution that meaningful increases in Venezuelan production could take years. Global oil prices are influenced by numerous factors, including OPEC+ policy, geopolitical conflicts, shipping disruptions and demand growth. Additional Venezuelan supplies could eventually place downward pressure on prices if production rises substantially, but the market impact will depend on the volume and timing of actual exports. The announcement nevertheless comes at a particularly important moment for global energy markets, with investors already watching supply risks associated with conflicts and disruptions elsewhere. Brent crude recently settled at $89.31 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate ended at $83.40, reflecting continued sensitivity to geopolitical and supply developments. A successful revival of Venezuelan production could provide an additional source of heavy crude for global markets and U.S. refiners. However, the gap between Venezuela’s enormous reserves and its current production capacity remains substantial. The agreement should therefore be viewed primarily as a long-term investment and geopolitical strategy rather than an immediate solution to high fuel prices. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

description.subtitle: Legal and Political Questions Remain
description.text: The announcement has also raised questions about the legal basis and political durability of the proposed arrangement. Trump provided limited details about the precise structure of the agreement, while Venezuela’s oil industry has historically been subject to strong state control and national ownership. Any major transfer of operational control to U.S. companies could therefore face legal and political challenges, particularly from Venezuelan groups concerned about national sovereignty and control over natural resources. The agreement is being negotiated with an interim government led by Delcy Rodriguez, adding another layer of uncertainty because Venezuela’s longer-term political structure remains unsettled. Supporters of the deal argue that private investment is necessary to restore the oil industry and generate revenue for Venezuelans after years of economic deterioration. Critics, however, may question whether an interim government should be able to approve such a far-reaching arrangement involving one of the country's most valuable strategic assets. The exact terms governing ownership, operating rights, revenue distribution and taxation will be crucial in determining whether the agreement can survive future political changes. Venezuela’s energy sector has previously experienced major shifts in policy, including nationalization and periods of increased foreign participation. The latest arrangement represents another significant change in that history. The Trump administration is betting that greater American involvement can stabilize production and create a mutually beneficial economic relationship. Yet the deal’s long-term success will depend on whether investors receive sufficient legal protection and whether Venezuelan institutions can maintain stable rules for foreign companies. The questions surrounding sovereignty and contractual authority could become particularly important if political opposition grows or future governments seek to renegotiate the terms. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}

description.subtitle: Strategic Importance for U.S. Energy Security
description.text: Beyond the commercial value of Venezuela’s oil, the agreement carries significant strategic implications for U.S. energy policy and Washington’s broader influence in the Western Hemisphere. Venezuela holds the largest proven crude oil reserves in the world, giving control over production and export infrastructure substantial geopolitical importance. Greater American involvement could reduce the influence of competing powers that have historically maintained economic relationships with Caracas, while creating a more direct supply channel between Venezuelan producers and U.S. refiners. The agreement also comes after Washington’s relationship with Venezuela underwent a dramatic transformation during 2026. The Trump administration has increasingly sought to reshape Venezuela’s political and economic direction while bringing its oil industry closer to American businesses. For the United States, access to additional heavy crude could be particularly valuable because some Gulf Coast refineries are designed to process heavier grades of petroleum. Increased Venezuelan supplies could therefore complement domestic U.S. production rather than simply compete with it. The initiative could also strengthen American influence over a critical energy producer located relatively close to the United States. For Venezuela, meanwhile, cooperation with U.S. companies offers a potential path toward rebuilding an industry that remains essential to government revenue and economic recovery. The two sides consequently have significant economic incentives to make the arrangement work. However, the geopolitical consequences could extend beyond energy markets. Other countries with longstanding commercial or political relationships with Venezuela may view greater U.S. control over the sector as a major strategic shift. The agreement could therefore reshape both Venezuela’s petroleum industry and the wider balance of influence surrounding one of Latin America’s most important energy producers. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

description.subtitle: Venezuela Faces a Long Road to Oil Recovery
description.text: The ultimate success of the agreement will depend on whether Venezuela can turn its enormous underground resources into reliable commercial production. The country’s reserves are immense, but reserve size alone does not guarantee high output. Years of underinvestment have damaged production facilities and reduced the efficiency of the wider petroleum system. Companies entering Venezuela will need to spend heavily on drilling, pipelines, processing facilities, ports and other infrastructure before substantial increases in exports can be achieved. The government will also need to establish predictable rules that encourage long-term investment while addressing questions about taxes, royalties and ownership. Venezuelan officials have presented the agreement as a pathway toward economic recovery, while Trump has emphasized its potential to strengthen U.S. energy security and lower fuel costs. Whether those promises materialize will depend largely on execution. If investment arrives at the projected scale and production increases significantly, Venezuela could regain an important position in global oil markets while generating billions of dollars in government revenue. U.S. companies could gain access to a major resource base and potentially secure additional supplies for American refineries. But if infrastructure problems, legal disputes or political instability slow investment, the expected benefits could take much longer to emerge. The agreement is therefore both a major energy initiative and a high-risk economic undertaking. Its announcement signals a fundamental change in the relationship between Washington and Caracas, placing Venezuela’s oil reserves at the center of a new U.S.-Venezuela economic strategy. For now, the scale of the proposed investment and the enormous reserves involved make the agreement one of the most consequential developments in global energy policy, even though many details remain to be finalized. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
